# Volume 2 — XIII A Golden Picnic

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

When Nell was traveling toward Pear Hill, she encountered Isolde, who was going to Grey Shutters, precisely at the place where the brook underneath the Whispering Wood was crossed by the moss-covered ancient log bridge, and the pair took a seat beside the edge of the Nymph’s Well, a spot where small ferns unfolded themselves in the manner of curly-haired green pixy creatures rousing from sleep.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0000 }

“Saturday is my birthday, and I was coming over right now to ask if you would help me mark the occasion,” said Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0001 }

“The day you were born? However, in March was when your birthday occurred!”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0002 }

“That wasn’t my fault,” Nell laughed. “Had my parents consulted me it would never have occurred at that time. Naturally, I should have chosen to be born in spring. Coming into the world alongside the mayflowers and violets must be delightful. One would always feel like their foster sister. Since I didn’t, however, celebrating my birthday in the spring is the next best thing. Saturday, Honora is coming over and Odette will be at home. All four of us will head off to the woods and spend a golden day getting acquainted with the spring. None of us really knows her yet, but back there we’ll meet her in a way we never can anywhere else. Anyhow, I want to explore all those fields and lonely places. I hold a conviction that scores of beautiful nooks exist there that have never truly been seen, even if they may have been looked at. We’ll form friendships with wind and sky and sun, and bring the spring home inside our hearts.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0003 }

“It seems terribly pleasant,” Isolde remarked, harboring a degree of secret skepticism regarding Nell’s verbal wizardry. “However, will it not still be extremely wet in certain spots?”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0004 }

“Oh, we can put on rubbers,” Nell conceded regarding practical matters. “And I need you to arrive early on Saturday morning so you can assist me in making lunch. My plan is to serve the most delicate items I can think of . . . foods that fit the spring season, if you catch my drift . . . small tarts filled with jelly and ladyfingers, alongside drop cookies covered in yellow and pink frosting, as well as buttercup cake. We also need to include sandwiches, even if they lack a certain poetry.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0005 }

Saturday turned out to be a perfect day for a picnic . . . a day filled with breeze and blue, warm, sunny, alongside a tiny playful wind sweeping over meadow and orchard. Across each sun-drenched upland and field lay a fragile, flower-starred green.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0006 }

As he harrowed at the rear of his farm, Mr. Pettifer, who felt a portion of the spring magic despite his sober, middle-aged blood, observed four girls carrying baskets as they lightly stepped over the edge of his field, right where it met a border of fir and birch woods. The sound of their merry laughter and voices reached him from a distance.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0007 }

“Isn’t it simple to feel joy when a day is like this?” Nell declared, possessing genuine Anneish philosophy. “Girls, let us attempt to turn this day into an exceptionally golden one, an occasion we are forever able to remember with pleasure. We must search for beauty and reject noticing all other things. ‘Begone, dull care!’ Odette, your mind is on a mishap from school yesterday.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0008 }

“By what means are you aware?” Odette breathed, filled with wonder.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0009 }

“Ah, I am familiar with that look . . . my own face has worn it frequently. However, do not dwell on it, sweetheart. It can wait until Monday . . . and if it fails to last that long, all the more preferable. Ah, girls, girls, look at that cluster of violets! It is a treasure for the mind’s art collection. At eighty years of age . . . should I reach that point . . . closing my eyes will allow me to view those violets precisely as they appear to me at this moment. Our day has bestowed its initial wonderful present upon us through them.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0010 }

“I believe that if it were possible to see a kiss, its appearance would resemble a violet,” Honora said.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0011 }

Nell beamed.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0012 }

“It brings me great joy that you voiced that idea, Honora, rather than merely contemplating it in silence. Life would be vastly more fascinating . . . even though it remains deeply fascinating as it is . . . if individuals openly declared their genuine opinions.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0013 }

“Certain people would find it far too scorching to maintain a grip,” wisely repeated Odette.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0014 }

“I guess that could be true, though they would only have themselves to blame for having unpleasant thoughts. Regardless, we are free to share every single thought today since our minds will hold only lovely ones. Everyone is allowed to speak whatever enters her mind. Conversation is simply that. I have not noticed this small trail until now. Let us go see where it leads.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0015 }

The trail meandered, its width so constrained that the young women moved one behind the other, and still the fir branches scraped against their faces. Soft, plush cushions of moss rested beneath the firs, and deeper along the way, in places where the trees grew smaller and sparser, the soil abounded with a diverse assortment of lush green vegetation.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0016 }

“What an abundance of elephant’s ears,” cried Isolde. “They are so lovely that I shall gather a large bouquet.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0017 }

“In what way did such elegant downy creations manage to acquire such a terrible title?” inquired Honora.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0018 }

“Since the individual who originally gave them a name lacked any imagination or possessed way too much,” Nell remarked, “Oh, girls, check that out!”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0019 }

“That” referred to a slight forest pond situated in the middle of a tiny grassy clearing where the track terminated. Further along in the season, it would be parched and its location occupied by a luxuriant patch of ferns; however, at present it was a shining quiet expanse, circular like a saucer and transparent as crystal. A circle of thin juvenile birches surrounded it, and small ferns bordered its edge.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0020 }

“How sweet!” Odette said.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0021 }

“Let us dance around it like wood-nymphs,” Nell exclaimed, setting down her basket and reaching out her hands.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0022 }

However, the dance failed to be successful because the earth was marshy and the rubbers belonging to Odette detached.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0023 }

“If you must wear rubbers, you are unable to be a wood-nymph,” she decided.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0024 }

“Indeed, a name must be given to this spot prior to our departure,” stated Nell, giving in to the unassailable truth of the situation. “Let each person offer a title, after which we will select one by chance. Isolde?”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0025 }

“Birch Pool,” Isolde offered without hesitation.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0026 }

“Crystal Lake,” Odette said.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0027 }

Positioned in their rear, Nell silently begged Honora through her gaze against committing an additional name like that, causing Honora to handle the situation by offering “Glimmer-glass.” The choice made by Nell was “The Fairies’ Mirror.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0028 }

Using a pencil that Schoolma’am Odette took from her pocket, the names were inscribed on pieces of birch bark and deposited inside Nell’s hat. After that, Honora closed her eyes and pulled one out. “Crystal Lake,” announced Odette victoriously. Crystal Lake became the chosen place, and even if Nell believed that fate had dealt the group a poor hand, she kept her thoughts to herself.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0029 }

Passing through the thicket past that point, the girls stepped into the fresh green privacy of Mr. Silas Mott’s rear field. Traversing it, they discovered the start of a path heading up into the forest and decided to investigate it too. Their exploration paid off with a series of lovely delights. To begin with, running along the edge of Mr. Mott’s field, there appeared a canopy of flowering wild cherry trees. The girls carried their hats by the straps on their arms and decorated their hair using the soft, pale flowers. Next, the path made a square turn and went deep into a forest of spruces that was so dense and dim that they proceeded through a dusk-like darkness, unable to catch even a patch of sky or ray of sun.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0030 }

“The wicked wood elves live in this place,” Nell murmured softly. “Although they are full of mischief and spite, they are unable to hurt us, since doing evil is forbidden to them during springtime. A single one was spying on us from behind that gnarled ancient fir; furthermore, didn’t you spot a cluster of them atop that large spotted toadstool we recently went by? The sunny spots are where the good fairies constantly reside.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0031 }

“I wish fairies actually existed,” Odette remarked. “Would it not be lovely if a person could have three wishes fulfilled . . . or perhaps just one? What wish would you make, girls, if a wish were granted to you? My wish would be for wealth, beauty, and intelligence.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0032 }

“I would desire to be slender and tall,” Isolde declared.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0033 }

“It would be my desire to achieve fame,” Honora expressed. Nell’s mind turned to her companion's hair, though she quickly rejected the notion, considering it unworthy.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0034 }

“I wish that it could be spring perpetually, within everyone’s heart and throughout all of our lives,” she remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0035 }

“However, that,” remarked Honora, “would simply be hoping for this world to resemble heaven.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0036 }

“Merely as one section of paradise. Summer and autumn would exist in the remaining areas . . . indeed, and a small amount of winter as well. Occasionally, I believe I desire sparkling snow-covered meadows and pale frosts in paradise. Wouldn't you agree, Odette?”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0037 }

“I . . . I don’t know,” Odette uttered in distress. A decent young woman and a churchgoer, Odette made a diligent effort to abide by her beliefs, accepting without question all the instruction she had received. Nevertheless, she avoided contemplating heaven as much as possible.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0038 }

“Posy Fay inquired of me recently whether our finest gowns would be worn daily when we are in heaven,” Isolde said with a laugh.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0039 }

“And weren’t you the one who told her that we would?” inquired Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0040 }

“Gracious, no! I informed her that we would not be giving any thought to dresses in that place.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0041 }

“Oh, I feel that we are going to . . . somewhat,” Nell stated with earnestness. “All eternity will afford us abundant time to do so while still attending to more crucial matters. It is my belief that every one of us will dress in gorgeous gowns . . . or perhaps raiment is a preferable term to use. During the initial few centuries, my desire will be to don pink . . . since I am certain it would require that much time for me to grow weary of it. I am so fond of pink, yet wearing it in this world is never possible for me.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0042 }

Beyond the spruces, the lane sloped downward to a bright, small clearing where a brook was crossed by a log bridge; after that appeared the magnificence of a sun-drenched beechwood whose air resembled clear golden wine, with leaves that were green and fresh, and a forest ground that formed a mosaic of flickering sunlight. Next were additional wild cherries, followed by a small valley containing flexible firs, and then a hill of such steepness that the girls became winded while ascending it; yet upon reaching its summit and stepping into the clear, they were met by the most charming surprise of everything.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0043 }

Further on lay the "back fields" belonging to the farms which extended to the upper Delford road. Immediately preceding them, enclosed by firs and beeches yet facing south, a small corner existed, containing a garden . . . or what used to be one. An dilapidated dyke made of stone, smothered in grass and mosses, encircled it. A line of garden cherry trees, as white as a snowdrift, stretched along the eastern side. Marks of former paths remained visible alongside a double row of rosebushes down the center; however, the remainder of the area formed a expanse of white and yellow narcissi, flowering in their lightest, most abundant, breeze-blown state over the rich green grasses.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0044 }

“Oh, how perfectly lovely!” exclaimed three of the girls. Nell merely looked on, her quietness speaking volumes.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0045 }

“How on earth did a garden ever come to exist behind this place?” Honora asked, astonished.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0046 }

“That has to be Dinah Wren’s garden,” Isolde said. “Mother has talked about it in my hearing, though it is my first time seeing it, and I wouldn’t have thought it was able to still exist. Have you heard the tale, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0047 }

“No, though that name sounds acquainted to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0048 }

“Ah, you have noticed it in the cemetery. Her grave is situated down in the corner by the poplars. You are familiar with that small brown monument featuring the sculpted opening gates and ‘Sacred to the memory of Dinah Wren, aged twenty-two.’ Beside her lies Jordan Wren, though he lacks a marker. I am surprised Thirza didn't mention it to you, Nell. Of course, thirty years have passed since it occurred, and it has slipped everyone's mind.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0049 }

“Well, if a story exists, we need to hear it,” Nell said. “We should sit down immediately in this spot surrounded by the narcissi so Isolde can relate it. Why, girls, hundreds of them are present . . . they have covered the entire area. The garden appears to be carpeted by a mixture of moonshine and sunshine. Making this discovery is truly worthwhile. Just consider that I have resided less than a mile away from this location throughout six years without ever laying eyes on it previously! Now, Isolde.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0050 }

“In the past,” Isolde started, “this property was owned by former Mr. David Gray. He resided elsewhere . . . at the location where Silas Mott resides today. A single son was born to him, named Jordan, who traveled to Boston during a particular winter for employment, and during his stay he became enamored with a woman called Dinah Murray. She was employed in a shop, an occupation she despised. Her childhood had been spent in the countryside, and her constant desire was to return there. Upon Jordan requesting her hand in marriage, her condition for agreeing was that he transport her to a peaceful location surrounded solely by fields and trees. Consequently, he conducted her to Brierley. Mrs. Sowerby remarked that his marriage to a Yankee constituted a terrible gamble, and undoubtedly Dinah possessed frail health and lacked housekeeping skills; nevertheless, my mother states she was extremely attractive and charming, and Jordan adored her completely. Eventually, Mr. Gray granted this farm to Jordan, who constructed a small dwelling back here where he and Dinah resided for a four-year period. She rarely ventured forth, and almost no individuals visited her apart from mother and Mrs. Sowerby. Jordan crafted this garden for her, which she adored passionately, occupying the majority of her time within it. Her domestic management was lacking, yet she possessed a talent for plants. Following this, illness struck her. Mother believes that consumption afflicted her prior to her arrival here. She was never fully bedridden, but continuously lost strength. Jordan refused to allow anyone else to attend to her. He performed every task personally, and mother indicates he showed tenderness and gentleness equal to a woman's. On a daily basis, he would enclose her in a shawl, convey her outdoors into the garden, and she would rest on a bench in full contentment. It is reported that she compelled Jordan to bow beside her each evening and dawn to join her in prayer, requesting that her eventual passing occur outside in the garden. This plea was granted. On a certain day, Jordan bore her out to the bench, gathered every blooming rose, and piled them upon her; she merely beamed up toward him . . . shut her eyes . . . and that,” Isolde quietly ended, “marked the finish.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0051 }

“Oh, that tale is so precious,” Nell murmured, dabbing her eyes to dry them.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0052 }

“What happened to Jordan?” Honora inquired.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0053 }

“Following the death of Dinah, he parted with the farm and returned to Boston. Mr. Jabez Mott purchased the property and relocated the small house to the roadside. Around a decade later, Jordan passed away, and his remains were returned to be interred next to Dinah.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0054 }

“I cannot comprehend how she might have desired to reside in this backwater, isolated from the rest of the world,” Odette remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0055 }

“Oh, I can easily comprehend that,” Nell remarked thoughtfully. “I wouldn’t desire it myself for a permanent arrangement, because, even though I love the woods and fields, I love people as well. However, I can comprehend it in Dinah. She was completely exhausted by the noise of the large city and the masses of individuals constantly arriving and departing and not caring at all about her. She merely wished to flee from everything to a quiet, green, welcoming place where she could find rest. And she received precisely what she desired, which is an achievement very few individuals accomplish, I think. She enjoyed four lovely years prior to her death. . . four years of complete joy, so I believe she should be envied rather than pitied. And then closing your eyes and drifting off to sleep amid roses, while the person you cherished most in the world smiles down upon you . . . oh, I believe it was lovely!”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0056 }

“Over there, those cherry trees were planted by her,” Isolde remarked. “She mentioned to mother that eating their fruit was something she would not survive to do, yet her desire was to believe that a thing she planted would remain alive and assist in rendering the world lovely once she had passed away.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0057 }

“I am very happy that we took this route,” stated Nell, whose eyes were shining. “You are aware that today is the anniversary of my adoption, and the gift it bestowed upon me for my birthday is this garden along with its history. Isolde, did your mother ever describe the appearance of Dinah Wren to you?”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0058 }

“No . . . merely that she possessed beauty.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0059 }

“I am quite pleased about that, since it allows me to picture her appearance without the limitation of reality. It is my belief that she was extremely slender and tiny, possessing gently wavy dark hair alongside large, gentle, shy brown eyes, as well as a small, pensive, fair face.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0060 }

The girls deposited their baskets in the garden of Dinah and passed the remainder of the afternoon wandering through the woods and fields encircling it, finding numerous pretty nooks and lanes. As hunger overtook them, they ate lunch in the most delightful spot of all . . . upon the precipitous bank of a murmuring brook where white birches rose from tall, feathery grasses. Sitting down among the roots, the girls did complete justice to the dainties of Nell, with even the unpoetical sandwiches being thoroughly enjoyed by robust, unspoiled appetites heightened by the abundance of fresh air and exercise they had experienced. Nell had supplied glasses and lemonade for her guests, though for her own share she consumed cold brook water out of a cup crafted from birch bark. The cup seeped, and the water possessed a flavor of earth, as brook water frequently does during spring; nevertheless, Nell considered it far more suited to the occasion than lemonade.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0061 }

“Listen, do you observe that poem?” she asked unexpectedly, gesturing.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0062 }

“In what place?” Odette and Isolde gazed intently, seeming to anticipate Runic inscriptions appearing upon the birch bark.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0063 }

“Over there . . . lower in the stream . . . that ancient green, moss-covered log with the current streaming over it in those even ripples that seem like they’ve been brushed, and that one beam of sunlight dropping straight across it, deep down into the water. Oh, it’s the loveliest poem I’ve ever seen.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0064 }

“I would describe it more as a picture,” Odette remarked. “Lines and verses make up a poem.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0065 }

“Indeed, I am not of that opinion.” Nell gave a firm negative nod of her head, which was crowned with a soft, untamed wreath of wild cherry. “A poem's outward clothing consists merely of its verses and lines, which are no truer representation of it than your own flounces and ruffles are of you, Odette. Within them lies the soul, which is the genuine poem . . . and that lovely fragment constitutes the soul of a poem yet to be composed. One does not behold a soul every day . . . even if it belongs to a poem.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0066 }

“I muse upon the appearance of a soul . . . an individual's soul . . .,” Honora remarked in a dreamy manner.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0067 }

“I would imagine it is similar to that,” Nell replied, indicating a beam of filtered sun rays pouring past a birch tree. “Naturally, it would possess a form and facial details as well. It pleases me to imagine that light forms our souls. Certain ones are completely penetrated by pinkish streaks and flickers . . . while others possess a gentle shimmer, similar to moonbeams upon the ocean . . . and others are faint and see-through, resembling morning fog.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0068 }

“I recall reading at some point that souls resembled flowers,” Honora remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0069 }

“In that case, your soul is a golden narcissus,” Nell said, “while Isolde’s resembles a red, red rose. The soul of Odette is an apple blossom, wholesome and sweet and pink.”
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0070 }

“And yours is a white violet, which has purple streaks at its center,” Honora concluded.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0071 }

Odette murmured to Isolde that she truly was unable to grasp the subject of their conversation, asking if she could.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0072 }

Under the glow of a serene, golden sunset, the girls walked home, carrying baskets packed with narcissus flowers from the garden of Dinah, portion of which were taken by Nell to the cemetery the following day and placed on the grave of Dinah. Musical robins whistled within the fir trees while frogs sang throughout the marshes. Topaz and emerald light filled every basin nestled amidst the hills.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0073 }

“Well, we have enjoyed ourselves tremendously, despite everything,” Isolde remarked, in a manner suggesting she had scarcely anticipated doing so upon her departure.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0074 }

“A truly golden day it has been,” Honora said.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0075 }

“I have a truly dreadful fondness for the woods, personally,” Odette remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0076 }

Nell remained silent. Looking off toward the western sky, she was remembering little Dinah Wren.
{: #nw-v02-c13-p0077 }
